catalog_quote: My analysis of the pitch accent differs from these works. High pitch (the prominence) in the citation form predictably falls on the penultimate syllable, an open syllable which may be light/mono-moraic (12) or heavy/bi-moraic vowel (13). (12) ... búna ‘coffee’ dondéʔe ‘cover of bamboo mak’ulánta ‘knife’ sagáda ‘slope’ wóʔo ‘water’ (13) buúro ‘butter’ duúna ‘mountain’ laága ‘ray, beam’ ... In words whose final syllables are heavy, the accent is placed on that bi-moraic vowel. Such words contain long vowels in their final syllables, the first vowel segment of the long vowel (i.e., the penultimate vowel segment) is accented, whereas its word-final vowel segment is not. Though, high pitch basically occurs on the penultimate vowel segments of inflected verbs, there are some verb suffixes whose final vowel segments are always accented. new_statements.quote: Note first that the data reveal a difference in the phonological stress, which I have distinguished as "dominant" vs "recessive" stress. The stress system of Hadiyya has not been analysed, and these are rather intuitive labels, with "Recessive" labelling stress without high pitch, and "Dominant" labelling stress accompanied by high pitch. [...] For the rather small number of feminine nouns, the same vowel occurs in both Cases. The difference between Comitative and Locative is then the purely prosodic one of stress.

new_statements.relation_note: Partial contradiction, no placement rule. The catalog (Tadesse Sibamo 2015, sec. 2.4 pp. 31-33) records a predictable high-pitch accent on the penultimate syllable/mora (on a heavy final syllable's first mora when the final vowel is long). Sim gives no rule and says the system is unanalysed; where he does place 'dominant' (high-pitch) stress, the locative stem-final vowel -ó- in mancónne, that is the penultimate syllable, which is consistent with the catalog's placement. But Sim's claim that the comitative -i-nne form carries stress WITHOUT high pitch, and that pitch/stress alone distinguishes Locative from Comitative on feminine nouns, makes the pitch contrastive, which the catalog source…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is given: Sim states outright that the stress system of Hadiyya 'has not been analysed'. What he reports is a two-way prosodic contrast he labels 'dominant' stress (stress accompanied by high pitch) vs 'recessive' stress (stress without high pitch), used to distinguish the Locative -o+nne (dominant stress on the stem-final vowel, e.g. mancónne 'on the man') from the Comitative/Instrumental -i+nne (recessive stress, mancinne 'with the man'), table (2.9b); for the few feminine nouns, where both cases end in -o+nne, the difference is 'purely prosodic'. Incidental remarks: a long penultimate ee is 'stressed' vs a short penultimate o 'unstressed' in the two subjunctives (p. 151); the cliticised auxiliary bee2e carries no stress, the preceding syllable does (p. 313 n. 1). Terminology treats the phenomenon as stress with high pitch as a concomitant feature, i.e. a stress-accent description, not a pitch accent analysis.
new_statements.exceptions: None in placement terms (no rule is given). Noted: the cliticised form bee2e 'lack' bears no stress (p. 313 n. 1); the Locative vs Comitative case endings on feminine nouns differ only by dominant vs recessive stress (p. 113).
new_statements.identity_note: Sim 1989 covers Hadiyya generally; the only dialect remark in the phonology note is that /z/ 'really occurs only in the Sooro speech area' (p. 13), and the stress remarks are not tied to a dialect. Tadesse 2015 (catalog source) is likewise general Hadiyya.

readall_conflicts: Sim 1989 (p. 113) vs the catalog source Tadesse Sibamo 2015 (pp. 31-33, 79): Sim describes a 'dominant' (stress + high pitch) vs 'recessive' (stress without high pitch) contrast that alone distinguishes Locative -o+nne from Comitative/Instrumental -i+nne (and for feminine nouns, two homophonous -o+nne endings), i.e. a contrastive prosodic difference, while explicitly stating that the stress system 'has not been analysed' and giving no placement rule. Tadesse rejects this ('My analysis of the pitch accent differs from these works'; 'I do not agree with the argumentation given by Sim (1989: 112-113) that pitch accent alone marks the distinction') and holds high pitch to be predictable on the penultimate syllable/mora, with a heavy (long-vowel) final syllable attracting it; Tadesse also lists Hudson 1976: 248 (stress on strong syllables: long vowels and/or closed syllables) among the analyses he departs from. The one location where Sim reports high pitch (the locative's stem-final vowel, the penult of mancónne) is compatible with Tadesse's penultimate placement, so the disagreement is about contrastiveness and type of prominence, not about where the high pitch sits in that form. Sim's own remark that a long penultimate ee is stressed while a short penultimate o is unstressed (p. 151) is not a rule and is compatible with either account.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding quotation, locator (sec. 2.4, pp. 31-33, exx. 12-15) and the exception quotation are all verbatim in the AAU-ETD PDF we hold/txt. Deciding source: a 2015 PhD documentation grammar, the most extensive and most recent description of Hadiyya in Glottolog's list; no phonology article, JIPA illustration, handbook chapter or instrumental study of Hadiyya prosody surfaced in Glottolog 5.1 (53 refs), Crossref, the AAU thesis repository, or the OHEL 2023 TOC, so the held source is probably the best available. Why 'adequate' rather than 'well-sourced': the accent section is two impressionistic pages, and the author himself reports that Hudson 1976 (weight incl. closed syllables) and Sim 1989 (morphologically distinctive dominant/recessive stress) analysed Hadiyya prominence differently; neither older source is held, and the record's contra/caution fields are empty.
